title: Apply blade-shearing skills and prepare blade-shearing equipment

lessons.title: Blade shears and how to prepare them
lessons.html:
Why blade shearing?

Blade shearing is shearing with hand shears (blades) instead of an electric machine. It is still used on many South African farms and in communal areas, especially in the Karoo and Eastern Cape. Blades leave a little more wool on the sheep, which protects it against cold after shearing. Blades are also used for crutching, eye-clipping and shearing goats and small flocks where there is no power.

Parts of blade shears

  • Blades - two cutting blades with sharp edges and points.
  • Bow - the spring at the back that opens the blades after each cut.
  • Handles - where the shearer grips; often bound with a strap or cord for a good grip.
  • Stop or nib - stops the blades from crossing too far.

Preparing the blades

  1. Check the blades for cracks, rust and bent points. Do not use damaged blades.
  2. Sharpen using a sharpening stone (whetstone). Hold the blade at the correct angle along the bevel and work evenly from heel to point. Keep the stone wet with water or oil as the maker recommends.
  3. Remove the burr from the flat inside face with light, flat strokes. Never grind the inside face hollow.
  4. Set the blades so they meet cleanly and cut along their full length. The blades must touch only along the cutting edges.
  5. Set the bow so the spring is not too stiff (tiring for the hand) or too weak (blades do not open).
  6. Test on a piece of wool or paper. Good blades cut cleanly without folding the fibres.

Care and safety

  • Keep blades in a sheath or tied shut when not in use.
  • Never leave blades lying open on the board or in the pens.
  • Clean and oil lightly at the end of the day to stop rust.
  • Clean and disinfect blades between flocks to prevent spreading infections.

lessons.title: Preparing sheep and the shearing area
lessons.html:
Planning the shearing day

Good preparation makes shearing faster, safer and gives better wool. The farm manager plans the date, the team and the pens. Shearing is usually done before the hot season and timed to avoid very cold, wet weather afterwards.

Preparing the sheep

  • Dry wool only. Never shear wet sheep. Wet wool can heat and rot in the bale and wet sheep chill easily. If rain is likely, pen sheep under cover the night before.
  • Empty stomachs. Keep sheep off feed for some hours before shearing, as the farm manager directs, but give water. A full rumen makes the sheep uncomfortable, causes more dung on the board and is harder on the shearer's back.
  • Sort the sheep by group, for example ewes, lambs and rams, so the wool from each group can be kept separate.
  • Crutch dirty sheep first to remove dung-stained wool (dags).
  • Do not shear heavily pregnant ewes roughly; handle them gently and follow the farm's programme.

Preparing the shed

  • Sweep the shearing board so it is clean and free of straw, dung and twine. Contamination such as plastic and twine lowers the wool price.
  • Prepare catching pens close to each shearer.
  • Set up the wool table, bins or bags for different wool types, and the wool press.
  • Have wound spray or antiseptic, a first-aid kit and clean water ready.

Health and safety

  • Lift and catch sheep with a straight back, using your legs.
  • Rest and stretch between sheep to protect your back and wrists.
  • Drink water often in a hot shed.
  • Report any cut on yourself straight away and keep wounds clean and covered.

lessons.title: Shearing technique and caring for the shorn sheep
lessons.html:
Holding the sheep

The sheep must be held so it is relaxed and the skin is tight where you cut. Set the sheep on its rump, leaning back against your legs. A sheep that is balanced and cannot get its feet on the ground struggles less. Use your free hand to stretch the skin in front of the blades.

Basic shearing pattern

The exact order is taught by your trainer, but most patterns follow these stages:

  1. Belly wool, kept separate.
  2. Crutch and inside of the hind legs.
  3. Hind leg and the rump.
  4. Neck and shoulder.
  5. Long blows along the side and back, then the second side.

Good blade work

  • Keep the bottom blade flat and close to the skin, points slightly down, so you cut near the skin without stabbing.
  • Make full, even cuts. Use the whole length of the blade.
  • Avoid second cuts - cutting the same place twice leaves short pieces of wool that lower the fleece value.
  • Take care on wrinkles, teats, the pizzle and around the eyes. Stretch the skin before cutting.
  • Keep the fleece in one piece where possible.

If the sheep is cut

Stop, check the wound and treat it with wound spray or antiseptic. Report deep cuts to the supervisor; a vet may need to stitch them. Fresh wounds attract blowflies, so check shorn sheep over the next days.

After shearing

  • Pick up the fleece, throw it on the wool table and skirt it (remove dirty edges) as the classer directs.
  • Release the sheep gently into a clean pen.
  • Shorn sheep lose body heat fast. Keep them close to shelter and extra feed if cold, wet weather is forecast.

Key points

  • Sharp, correctly set blades cut cleanly and are less tiring.
  • Shear only dry sheep with empty stomachs.
  • Keep the board clean to avoid wool contamination.
  • Keep the blade flat to the skin and avoid second cuts.
  • Treat cuts at once and protect shorn sheep from cold.
